title: Cap table basics: a worked example from founders to Series A
excerpt: How a startup cap table changes from founding to Series A: ESOP pool, SAFE or CCPS conversion, seed and Series A dilution, with every calculation shown.

sources.claim: Post-money SAFE: ownership = investment / cap; cap is post existing pool, not post new pool; SAFEs diluted by priced round
Cap table definition; common vs preferred; liquidation preference; keep records updated
Fully diluted shares formula and why ownership is best viewed fully diluted
Pools start ~10% pre-seed; median grows 1-1.5% per round
Last 6 months, software: seed $24.3M on $4.1M, 18% dilution; Series A $80M on $14.4M, 18%; 1,000+ rounds
Option pool shuffle: $8M pre with 20% pool is effectively $6M; size pool to hiring plan
CCPS conversion formula fixed upfront; FEMA NDI floor at FMV for foreign investors; 20-year limit; 10-year backstop
Rule 12: special resolution; 1-year minimum grant-to-vest; promoters and >10% directors excluded
Start-up exception for promoter ESOPs extended from 5 to 10 years; SEBI June 2025 change for founders at IPO

content:
A cap table (capitalisation table) is the list of who owns how much of a company, counting shares, options and anything that can convert into shares. The fastest way to understand it is to build one: below, two founders go from 100% at incorporation to about 47% combined after an option pool, a SAFE, a seed round and a Series A, with every step of arithmetic shown.

The numbers matter more than usual this year. Carta's data for the first half of 2026 shows founders selling a median 18% at seed and 18% at Series A, while seed and Series A valuations have never been higher, so small changes in terms (how the option pool is counted, what a SAFE cap means) can move founder ownership more than headline valuation does. This piece is an educational model, not legal, tax or investment advice; have a lawyer or chartered accountant check your own documents.

Key takeaways

  • Always count ownership on a fully diluted basis: issued shares plus options, the unallocated pool and convertibles as if converted.
  • A post-money SAFE sells ownership equal to investment divided by cap ($500,000 at a $5 million cap is 10%), but that stake is then diluted by the priced round and any new pool.
  • When the option pool is created or topped up inside the pre-money valuation, founders and earlier investors bear its cost, not the new investor.
  • In our example, two founders own 47.08% together after Series A; each round costs them a little more than the headline percentage sold.
  • Indian startups get SAFE-like economics through compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS), with FEMA pricing rules for foreign investors.

What a cap table records

Carta describes the cap table as the single record of a company's ownership: each shareholder, how many shares they hold, the type of equity and any convertible instruments such as SAFEs or convertible notes, according to Carta's founder guide. Founders and employees usually hold common shares, while investors hold preferred shares that typically carry a liquidation preference, meaning they are repaid before common shareholders in a sale.

The figure that matters for negotiation is the fully diluted share count. Carta defines it as common shares outstanding plus convertible securities, stock options, warrants and the option pool, and says ownership is most accurately thought of on that basis, according to Carta. Every percentage below is fully diluted.

Step 1: incorporation

Two co-founders, Asha and Ben, incorporate and issue themselves 5,000,000 shares each. The company has 10,000,000 shares, and each founder owns 50%.

Step 2: creating an employee option pool

Before raising money, the founders reserve shares for future hires. Carta's data shows pre-seed companies typically start their pools at about 10%, with the median growing by roughly 1-1.5 percentage points each round, according to Carta.

To make the pool exactly 10% of the new total, the founders' 10,000,000 shares must be 90% of it:

  • New total = 10,000,000 ÷ 0.90 = 11,111,111 shares
  • Pool = 11,111,111 − 10,000,000 = 1,111,111 shares

Each founder now holds 45% (5,000,000 ÷ 11,111,111). The pool is reserved, not issued; options granted from it still count in the fully diluted total.

Step 3: a pre-seed SAFE

An angel invests $500,000 on Y Combinator's post-money SAFE with a $5 million post-money valuation cap. YC's user guide explains that ownership sold under a post-money SAFE is the investment divided by the cap, so $500,000 ÷ $5,000,000 = 10%, according to Y Combinator. The guide also says the cap is "post" the existing options and pool, but not post any new or increased pool adopted in the priced round, and that SAFEs are diluted by the new money in that round.

The SAFE converts when the company raises a priced round. Its share count is the number that equals 10% of the capitalisation including those shares:

  • SAFE shares = 11,111,111 ÷ 0.90 − 11,111,111 = 1,234,568
  • Capitalisation after conversion = 12,345,679 shares
  • Effective SAFE price = $5,000,000 ÷ 12,345,679 = about $0.405 a share

At this point the founders hold 81% together (10,000,000 ÷ 12,345,679), the pool 9% and the SAFE holder 10%. For more on how SAFEs work and their Indian equivalents, see our SAFE notes explainer.

Step 4: the seed round, and the option pool shuffle

A seed fund offers $3 million at a $12 million pre-money valuation, so $15 million post-money, buying 20% ($3m ÷ $15m). It asks for the option pool to equal 10% of the company after the round, counted inside the pre-money valuation.

That last condition is the "option pool shuffle", a term described by the Venture Hacks blog in 2007. Its example: a stated $8 million pre-money that includes a new 20% pool on a $10 million post-money is really a $6 million valuation of the company the founders built, according to Venture Hacks. Its advice is to size the pool to an actual hiring plan rather than accept a round number.

Here is how the seed round works out. After the round, the investor owns 20% and the pool 10%, so everything else (founders plus SAFE, 11,234,568 shares) is 70%:

  • Post-money total = 11,234,568 ÷ 0.70 = 16,049,383 shares
  • Seed investor shares = 20% × 16,049,383 = 3,209,877
  • Pool target = 10% × 16,049,383 = 1,604,938, so a top-up of 493,827 shares
  • Price per share = $3,000,000 ÷ 3,209,877 = about $0.935
  • Check: pre-money shares (16,049,383 − 3,209,877 = 12,839,506) × $0.935 = $12.0 million
HolderShares after seedFully diluted %
Asha (founder)5,000,00031.15%
Ben (founder)5,000,00031.15%
SAFE holder1,234,5687.69%
Seed investor3,209,87720.00%
Option pool1,604,93810.00%
Total16,049,383100%

The SAFE holder bought 10% but now owns 7.69%, because the seed money and the pool top-up dilute everyone in the pre-money. The founders sold 20% to the seed fund but fell from 81% to 62.31%, a 23% relative drop, because they also absorbed the pool top-up. The SAFE got its shares at about $0.405, less than half the seed price, which is the reward for investing earlier.

Step 5: the Series A

Eighteen months later, a lead investor offers $10 million at a $40 million pre-money valuation ($50 million post-money), again for 20%. This time the pool must be 12% after the round, in line with Carta's observation that pools grow by about one to one-and-a-half points per round. Some of the pool has been granted to employees by now, but granted options stay in the fully diluted count, so the arithmetic is unchanged.

Everyone except the new investor and the pool (founders, SAFE and seed: 14,444,445 shares) must equal 68%:

  • Post-money total = 14,444,445 ÷ 0.68 = 21,241,831 shares
  • Series A shares = 20% × 21,241,831 = 4,248,366
  • Pool target = 12% × 21,241,831 = 2,549,020, a top-up of 944,082 shares
  • Price per share = $10,000,000 ÷ 4,248,366 = about $2.354

Asha5,000,00023.54%$11.77 million
Ben5,000,00023.54%$11.77 million
SAFE holder1,234,5685.81%$2.91 million
Seed investor3,209,87715.11%$7.56 million
Series A investor4,248,36620.00%$10.00 million
Option pool2,549,02012.00%$6.00 million
Total21,241,831100%$50.0 million

Paper value is not cash. Investors' preferred shares usually carry a liquidation preference, so in a modest sale the founders' common shares can be worth far less than this table suggests.

How the founders' stake shrank, round by round

StageFounders combinedWhat caused the change
Incorporation100%Only founder shares exist
Option pool90.00%10% reserved for hires
SAFE converts81.00%10% sold at the $5m cap

Compare the example with real medians. Carta's benchmarks from more than 1,000 software rounds in the six months to July 2026 show a median seed of $4.1 million raised at a $24.3 million valuation with 18% dilution, and a median Series A of $14.4 million at an $80 million valuation, also 18%, according to Carta. Carta's analyst Peter Walker notes that medians are only the middle of a wide range. Our example sells 20% per round to keep the arithmetic round.

Use your metrics to judge whether a round's dilution is worth it: what the money buys in runway and growth. Our startup metrics guide explains burn, runway and the other numbers investors check, and the funding tracker lists recent rounds.

The same cap table in India: CCPS and ESOP rules

Indian companies cannot simply issue a US SAFE, so early rounds usually use compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS). The arithmetic above still applies, but the legal plumbing differs:

  • Conversion formula. The conversion ratio is fixed in the subscription agreement at the start, typically using a valuation cap, a discount or both, according to Treelife.
  • FEMA price floor. For foreign investors, the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019 stop conversion below the fair value set when the CCPS were issued, which limits fully open-ended pricing, Treelife says.
  • Time limit. Treelife notes that the Companies Act caps preference share tenure at 20 years, and that many CCPS-based SAFE structures set a 10-year backstop for conversion.

Indian ESOP rules also shape the pool. Under rule 12 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014, an unlisted company needs a special resolution of shareholders to adopt an employee stock option scheme, there must be at least one year between grant and vesting, and promoters, and directors holding more than 10% of equity, cannot receive options, according to the rule's text on ca2013.com. Start-ups have an exception: they can grant options to promoters for up to ten years from incorporation, a window later extended from five years, according to law firm Vinod Kothari Consultants. The same firm notes that SEBI's board approved a change in June 2025 so that founders classified as promoters at IPO can still exercise options granted at least one year before the IPO decision.

Common cap table mistakes

  • Counting only issued shares. Percentages that ignore the pool and convertibles overstate founder ownership.
  • Ignoring the pool's position. A pool inside the pre-money is a cost to existing holders; model it before you sign.
  • Stacking SAFEs without a model. Each post-money SAFE dilutes founders directly, and several caps add up quickly.
  • Oversized pools. Size the pool to a real hiring plan, as Venture Hacks suggests.
  • Stale records. Carta's guide stresses updating the table after every grant, exercise and round, since investors review it in diligence.

Bottom line

A cap table is simple division done carefully and repeatedly. The details that move founder ownership most are not the headline valuation but the fully diluted count, the size and timing of the option pool, and how convertibles are capped. Build the model in a spreadsheet before every raise and check each investor's numbers against your own.

FAQ

What is a fully diluted cap table?

A table counting all issued shares plus options, the unallocated pool and convertibles as if converted. Term sheets usually quote ownership on this basis.

How much equity should founders give up at seed?

There is no rule. Carta's median for software seed rounds in the first half of 2026 was 18%.

Does a SAFE dilute founders before it converts?

Economically yes: a post-money SAFE fixes the percentage sold at investment divided by cap, though shares are issued only at conversion.

Who bears the option pool top-up?

If it sits in the pre-money valuation, existing holders do: founders, and holders of earlier SAFEs or shares.

Can Indian founders get ESOPs?

Generally no if they are promoters, but start-ups may grant them for up to ten years from incorporation under the Companies Act rules.
